Description: Some minerals can take up and give out electrons without their structure changing, a bit like a rechargeable battery. We call them biogeobatteries. They are mixed-valence minerals, which means they contain iron or other elements in more than one charge state. Examples include iron oxides, clays, sulphides and green rust. These minerals are widespread underground and may drive significant transfers of energy. Our work aims to understand how microbes access these minerals. This could unlock their potential for low-cost, low-power energy storage in remote places.

Iron minerals such as magnetite and ferrihydrite can bind metals to their surfaces and lock them in place. We test iron minerals made by microbes (biogenic) and those formed without them (abiogenic). We measure how well they capture critical metals, which are metals vital to modern technology, such as cobalt, zinc and vanadium. We also test how well they capture toxic contaminants such as arsenic, chromium and cadmium. The aim is to develop new ways to recover resources from waste and to improve how polluted water is cleaned up.

Techniques such as Mössbauer spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction help us identify the minerals in a sample. Mössbauer spectroscopy uses gamma rays to probe iron atoms. Raman spectroscopy uses laser light. X-ray diffraction reveals how atoms are arranged in a crystal. We are developing new methods for analysing the data from these techniques through a web-based platform. It will combine users' own data with growing databases, so that both simple and complex samples can be analysed and interpreted quickly.

Some bacteria gain energy from iron, and in doing so they produce magnetic minerals. We want to explain how this happens in the environment and how it is linked to climate change. High rainfall creates anoxic conditions, meaning there is little or no oxygen. These conditions suit iron-reducing bacteria, which form magnetite. When rainfall is low, oxygen is present, the bacteria slow down or stop, and little magnetite forms. As a result, changes in the magnetic properties of soils and sediments can be used as a record of past rainfall in different environments.
